catalog_quote: En general el acento en yanesha', o sea el lugar donde recae la mayor intensidad de voz y tono alto, se determina por el tipo de sílaba. Aquí se presenta una escala de fuerza o peso silábico ... Escala de fuerza o peso silábico (C)VV(C) (C)Vh(C) (C)VC fuertes / más fuerte ... (C)V'(C) (C)V débiles / más débil ... nótese que no se emplea la tilde en el diccionario, ni en los ejemplos de esta gramática, ya que las reglas predicen el lugar de la mayor fuerza de voz ... Las reglas de acentuación son las siguientes: 1. En general el acento recae en las sílabas fuertes. ... 2. Pero puesto que la primera sílaba ma' es más fuerte en la escala que la sílaba pa, ma' recibe el acento en [má'pa]. ... 3. Puesto que todas las sí…

new_statements.quote: [sec. 0.2, p. 191] Amuesha has 9 vowel phonemes ... 22 consonant phonemes ... and a phoneme of stress /’/. [sec. 3, p. 194] 3. Stress appears to be phonemic, although no conclusive contrastive pairs have thus far been discovered. Stress tends to occur on the penult: awaéé-kma early. It may, however, occur on the ultima: wawankeSya4 bat. Less frequently it is antepenultimate: né‘motap” I visit you. In some words there appears to be free fluctuation in stress placement: o-tén ~ 6é-éen comb. In some words there appears to be fluctuation in stress placement according to occurrence in context as contrasted with occurrence in isolation. ... Further investigation may reveal some correlation between stress and long vowels, or between stress and sentence rhythm.

new_statements.relation_note: Type differs from the catalog record: Duff-Tripp 1997 (sec. 9.7) makes stress predictable from a syllable-weight scale ((C)VV(C), (C)Vh(C), (C)VC strong vs (C)V'(C), (C)V weak) and writes no accent marks because 'las reglas predicen el lugar'; Fast 1953 instead posits a stress phoneme with penult as the commonest but not rule-governed position (also ultima, antepenult, free fluctuation). The conflict is soft: Fast calls his analysis provisional ('no conclusive contrastive pairs', 'further investigation may reveal some correlation between stress and long vowels'), which is the direction Duff-Tripp's later weight analysis took; Fast 1953 is the earlier, superseded statement and does not by it…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Fast lists 'a phoneme of stress' in the inventory (sec. 0.2) and in sec. 3 treats stress as apparently phonemic while admitting that no conclusive contrastive pairs had been found: stress mostly falls on the penult, but also on the ultima and, less often, the antepenult; some words fluctuate freely, and placement can differ between isolation and sentence context. He closes by suggesting that further work may reveal a correlation between stress and long vowels or sentence rhythm, i.e. he leaves open that placement is conditioned by vowel length (the weight analysis later given by Duff-Tripp 1997). A tentative, hedged statement: stress location not predicted by any rule he states, penult the commonest position.
new_statements.exceptions: ultima stress (e.g. 'bat'), antepenult stress (e.g. 'I visit you'), free fluctuation in some words ('comb'), and isolation-vs-context differences ('other' vs 'other dog comes'); possible correlation with long vowels and sentence rhythm left for further investigation
new_statements.identity_note: Fast 1953 describes Amuesha (= Yanesha', ISO ame), the same language as the catalog record; no dialect information obtained since the article was not read.

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation, the domain quotation (rule 3) and the exception quotation (rule 8) are all verbatim in the SLP 43 scan we hold at pp.152-156, confirmed by scanned text and by reading p.153 as a page scan. (2) The classification rests on the language's only reference grammar (Duff-Tripp 1997/2008, 283 pp), whose sec. 9.7 is a dedicated stress section with a five-step weight scale, primary stress on the last strongest syllable, penult preference under ties, and listed exceptions; the catalog's 'weight-hedged', what counts as heavy: CVV+CVC, edge unbounded, the exceptions statement listed-set coding matches the text. (3) No better source exists per Glottolog 5.1, CrossRef, PUCP theses, StressTyp2 and WALS source lists: the alternatives are Fast 1953 (4-page IJAL phoneme note, older), an unlocatable 1985 'Fonología yanesha' ms., and 1905/1929 missionary sketches; no instrumental or JIPA study was found. sources.note: Only other published phonological statement on the language; reportedly treats stress as (near-)phonemic with a penultimate tendency, which is the one description that could bear on the weight-sensitive (tentative) flag (Duff-Tripp's rule 5 fluctuation and rule 8 exceptions). Older and far shorter than the held grammar, so it cannot displace it.

The catalog record for Yanesha' has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this work adds nothing on stress. It is a community-development reader (Glottolog's 'grammar' source_kind is a misclassification), and the copy SIL archives is the 1996 third edition of the 1970 title. A full-text search of the scanned for acent-, tilde, tónic-, tono, sílaba, énfasis found no hits; the only 'pronunci-' hits are the segmental letter descriptions quoted.
